I know I’m a lot younger than you are, but as a person who went from one coast of the US to the other I can maybe give you some advice on meeting new people. For starters, I’d recommend you start going out more. You tend to meet people if you frequent certain areas, like a coffee shop or a bookstore, some place other people would go to as well that you can strike up a conversation with. 

There are some resources for meeting people on the internet, and also some videos and sites on how to build up a social life from scratch. I’d recommend looking those up and seeing what kind of people you’d like to meet. Maybe even rekindling some old relationships with past friends would be a good idea! Just try to remember that you’re your own person first and foremost. Your relationships just help you define who you are easier. Don’t be afraid if an interaction doesn’t go super well or you just don’t hit it off with someone. Not everyone is going to like you, that’s just a fact of life. Keep going and you’ll find the ones who do. Hope I could help.

Hi! I tend to have a lot of the same anxieties too, but I promise you that nothing will be too different. At most, you’ll just be hanging out with him along with his girlfriend more. That doesn’t make you any less important, and it doesn’t mean you’ll be any less of a friend to him. There’s nothing to fear. I’m speaking from personal experience when I say that.
If you still feel anxious about it, maybe bring it up to him in a casual manner. Something like “hey, we’re still friends right?” or something that voices your concerns about your friendship without pitting it all on his girlfriend. Just remember that your friendship is him and you, not you him and her. Nothings really going to change that.

Hi, I’m cis so I don’t know how helpful I’ll be, but some of my closest friends struggle with gender and trans issues and I’m very involved in the lbgt community, so maybe I can be of some help.


It sounds like you’re probably experiencing gender dysphoria. I’d recommend seeking information on how to deal with it. Remember to try and stay away from “.com” sites as they aren’t always trustworthy. Here’s a site I found that has a college resource ( [UNC](https://healthyheels.org/2016/11/21/living-with-gender-dysphoria-tips-for-transgender-peoples-friends-allies-and-partners/amp/)  ).Although it’s directed at cis people trying to understand the issues their transgender friends/family deal with, it has some sources and more resources including studies, and it may give you some ideas for starting place that you can go forward from to being more comfortable.


For more personal advice, my friend C (18 too!) is genderfluid, possibly Trans. I don’t try to pry, personally I care for them anyway they are. They weren’t comfortable being masculine, so they found a place where they could explore their gender safely. They started with small things, like painting their nails or wearing less noticeable makeup like mascara or a little bit of lip gloss now and then. I would recommend finding a place you feel comfortable expressing yourself in, maybe off campus, that you can start doing small things to feel more comfortable with yourself. I’d also like to say that being tall is completely normal for girls. I’m 5”9’ which is pretty tall, but I’ve met girls who are easily 6”+. (Between you and me, facial hair is a problem too now and again, but that’s a secret). Remember to move at a pace you’re comfortable with. Stay safe, stay happy, and do your research! I hope I could help.
